background.definition: Mastitis is an inflammation of the breast and infective mastitis is breast inflammation believed to be caused by bacteria. Mastitis can be lactational or non-lactational – the latter further classified as periductal mastitis (inflammation of the subareolar ducts) and idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM). A breast abscess is a localized collection of pus surrounded by inflamed breast tissue; the majority (85%) are non-lactational.

list.listitem: Lactation mastitis has been reported in 2% to 27% of breastfeeding women. In a study conducted at two maternity hospitals in Melbourne, Australia in 2009-2011, 20% of 346 women developed mastitis.
Authors of a systematic review found 11 episodes per 1000 breastfeeding weeks, with the greatest incidence in the first 4 weeks.
Breast abscesses have been reported in 5% to 11% of mastitis cases.
Mastitis results in an average of 4.9 restricted days and 1 bed day.

Among women with human immunodeficiency virus (HIV), recurrent severe subclinical mastitis was associated with significantly increased odds of shedding cell-free HIV-1 in breast milk (OR: 5.2; 95%CI 1.7-15.6).
Usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus.
Less often caused by coagulase-negative staphylococci, Escherichia coli, Bacteroides species, or Group A and B beta-hemolytic streptococci.
Milk stasis is believed to an important initiating event.

In a retrospective study of 108 patients with breast infections occurring over 4 years at a single institution, 47 (43.5%) had primary abscesses, 49 (45.4%) were post-operative surgical site infections and 12 (11.1%) were lactational. Although the most common isolate was Staphylococcus aureus (cultured in 16.7% of primary abscesses and 24% of surgical site infections), infections were frequently polymicrobial.

Periductal mastitis primarily affects patients of child-bearing age who are smokers or those who have breast scarring from previous radiation or surgery; the majority are bacterial including Staphylococci, Enterococci, and anaerobic Streptococci.

Authors of a systematic review of non-lactational infectious mastitis found 47 papers describing 93 cases. Bacteria were the most common etiology, present in 73 cases, and included 28 cases of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, 15 case of Corynebacterium species and 13 cases of non-tuberculous mycobacteria.

IGM is a rare, benign inflammatory breast disease, but can mimic breast carcinoma both clinically and radiologically. Infectious agents that have been identified in cases of granulomatous mastitis include actinomyces species and Corynebacterium species.

Actinomycosis is a gram-positive, facultatively anaerobe that rarely can cause granulomatous mastitis and abscess formation. Actinomyces species were isolated from 11 breast samples from abscesses referred to the Anaerobe Reference Unit, Cardiff, Wales, between 1988 and 2014; an Actinomyces-like organism was identified in one additional abscess. Ten of the 12 women had chronic, recurrent infections (mean, 2.8 episodes), some recurred over many years.
The pathogenic organisms may gain entrance through a crack or an abrasion of the nipple.
Breast abscess may develop if mastitis treatment is delayed, incorrect, or ineffective.
Risk factors for mastitis are shown in the table below.
Inadequate drainage is also cited as a predisposing factor; this may be due to factors including plugged ducts, inadequately managed engorgement, poor infant attachment, and weaning.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: History of mastitis with previous child
Cracks and nipple sores in the same week as mastitis
Using an antifungal cream in the same 3-week interval as mastitis
Using a manual breast pump (for women with no prior history of mastitis)
Expression of breast milk several times daily
Presence of S. aureus on the nipple
Presence of S. aureus in the breastmilk

list.listitem: Authors of a Cochrane review found limited evidence of effectiveness for any preventive strategy with no benefit from breastfeeding education, pharmacological treatments (ie, antibiotics, mupirocin, fusidic acid ointment) and alternative therapies (ie, antisecretory factor cereal) on the occurrence of mastitis. However,authors of a meta-analysis of 4 RCTs found that a single dose of oral azithromycin reduced rates of postpartum mastitis or breast abscess (RR 0.6, 95% CI 0.4-0.8).

In an Italian open randomized parallel controlled trial of 208 women, those randomized to biological nurturing, a neurobehavioral approach to breastfeeding support that encourages women to breastfed in a relaxed, laidback position, had fewer breast problems including cracked nipples (RR 0.42, 95% CI 0.24-0.74).

The World Health Organization (WHO) suggests frequent breast feeding, optimizing breastfeeding technique, prompt attention to milk stasis with increased feedings and use of heat prior to feedings, gentle massage of lumpy areas and hand expression of milk as needed; data are lacking.
Other measures such as rest and adequate fluid and nutrition are felt to be important.
Patients with mastitis have clinical signs and symptoms of inflammation. C
When an abscess is suspected clinically, ultrasound does not confirm it in up to 50% of cases. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Often bilateral; no fever or erythema

list.listitem: Patients with mastitis have clinical signs and symptoms of inflammation: breast pain, chills, myalgias, and fever.
The breast examination in mastitis typically shows unilateral edema, erythema in a wedge-shaped area, and tenderness.
In breast abscess, examination shows a tender, hard breast mass, possibly fluctuant, with erythema.

Detection of pathogens in breast milk is not always possible and milk culture is not suggested for guiding initial therapy. Bacteria are often found in breast milk from asymptomatic breasts and 50% of milk cultures may be sterile.

The WHO suggests breast milk culture can be performed selectively in women with hospital-acquired cases, severe or unusual cases, failure to respond to antibiotics in 2 days, or recurrence. Breast milk culture is also suggested for abscess.
Ultrasound is often used when abscess is suspected. In clinically-suspected cases, an abscess was not detected by ultrasound in 34% to 50% of patients.

Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM) is diagnosed histologically. Findings favoring IGM over carcinoma on ultrasound are multiple irregular hypoechoic masses and collections with tubular connections with fingerlike aspects and fistulae formation to the skin in patients with breastfeeding history.
Polymerase chain reaction for Mycobacterium tuberculosis using specimens obtained during fine needle aspiration may be helpful in diagnosing tuberculosis abscess.
Mastitis is diagnosed by history and physical examination, which indicates inflammation.
Ultrasonography can be helpful for detecting abscess formation but does not confirm it in up to 50% of clinically-suspected cases.

Authors of a Cochrane review found no high quality studies of antibiotic therapy for lactation mastitis. Antibiotics that cover staphylococci and streptococci are usually prescribed for 10 to 14 days. C

For patients with idiopathic granulomatous mastitis (IGM), surgery or high-dose steroids appear successful in most patients with addition of methotrexate considered for resistant or recurrent cases. B

With respect to breast abscess in breastfeeding women, authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine whether needle aspiration was more effective than incision and drainage or whether an antibiotic should be routinely prescribed to women undergoing drainage. C
Most small abscesses can be treated with ultrasound-guided needle aspiration. Others are treated with incision and drainag and antibiotics. C
Lactation should be continued to allow for proper drainage of the breast. B

The WHO suggests treatment with antibiotics in cases where there is a positive breast milk bacterial culture, symptoms are severe at onset, a nipple fissure is visible, or symptoms do not improve after 12 to 24 hours of improved milk removal.
If MRSA infection is unlikely and treatment is outpatient: dicloxacillin 500 mg orally 4 times daily or cephalexin 500 mg orally 4 times daily.
If MRSA infection is unlikely and treatment is inpatient: nafcillin or oxacillin 2 g IV every 4 hours.

If MRSA infection is possible and treatment is outpatient: trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole double strength 1 to 2 tablets orally twice daily or clindamycin 300 mg orally 4 times daily (if susceptible). Doxycycline 100 mg twice daily can also be considered. Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole may cause increased bilirubin and should be used with caution in mothers of premature, ill, hyperbilirubinemic and G6PD-deficient infants. Doxycycline is generally avoided in lactating mothers.

If MRSA infection is possible and treatment is inpatient: vancomycin 1 g IV every 12 hours. Combination vancomycin with a beta-lactam-beta-lactamase (i.e., ampicillin-sulbactam) or third-generation cephalosporin (e.g., ceftriaxone) in combination with metronidazole provides coverage for gram negative and anaerobic pathogens and may also be appropriate.

Authors of one review noted that MRSA accounts for 8-12% of breast abscesses, with risk factors including recent hospitalization or surgery, HIV infection, injection drug use, or prior antibiotic use.
Although the optimal length of antibiotic treatment is not known, 10 to 14 days is frequently prescribed.
In addition to drainage, antibiotic therapy appropriate for Actinomyces species includes oral penicillin or amoxicillin and, if recurrent, should continue for 6 or more weeks.
Supportive therapy should be used, such as pain medication and an antiinflammatory medication.

Authors of a systematic review of 15 studies of IGM treatment found pooled estimates for complete remission/resolution of 90.6% (95% CI 83.8%-95.7%) for surgery, 71.8% (95% CI 67.1%-76.3%) for oral steroids, and 94.5% (95% CI 88.9%-98.3%) for combined surgery and oral steroids. Pooled estimates for recurrence rates were 6.8%, 20.9%, and 4.0%, respectively .

Two-month treatment with high-dose prednisolone (50 mg for three days followed by 25 mg for three days, 12.5 mg for three days, and 5 mg daily afterwards) resulted in a higher remission rate than low-dose prednisolone (5 mg daily) in an RCT of 30 patients with IGM (93.3% vs. 53.3%, respectively). Interestingly, topical steroids performed as well as systemic steroids in another RCT with 124 patients; complete clinical regression occurred in 90 (83.3%) patients.

In an RCT of 36 patients with IGM, intralesional steroid administration was as successful as systemic steroid administration, with 32 patients experiencing complete clinical regression. Intralesional or topical steroids were both demonstrated as effective by authors of a meta-analysis of 8 trials including 613 patients; in addition, there were fewer side effects but similar recurrence rates compared with systemic treatment.

In an RCT of 318 patients with resistant or recurrent IGM, combination methotrexate and low-dose corticosteroids showed higher rates of complete response compared with either prednisolone or supportive care (94.3% vs. 14.1% and 0%, respectively).

Recurrence of granulomatous mastitis was examined across 65 studies with authors concluding that the lowest recurrence rate of 4% was seen with combination methotrexate and corticosteroids. Recurrence rates ranging from 7-13% were shown for topical steroid use, methotrexate use, observation, excision, steroid use and surgery, antibiotic and steroid use; the highest recurrence rate was for drainage alone (65%).
Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis of 19 studies with 1044 patients found a success rate of 81% among patients with mild periprosthetic breast infection treated with antibiotics alone.
Ultrasound-guided needle aspiration has become the preferred approach to treating breast abscesses. Local anesthesia and an 18 gauge needle are recommended.
Incision and drainage should be considered if aspiration fails after 3 to 5 attempts.
Abscesses that are 3 cm or larger and are multi-loculated are more likely to require incision and drainage.

Authors of a Cochrane review found insufficient evidence to determine whether needle aspiration was more effective than incision and drainage or whether an antibiotic should be routinely prescribed to women undergoing drainage.
Ultrasound-guided percutaneous catheter placement may be considered for treatment of larger abscesses (>3 cm).

Among 1044 patients with periprosthetic breast infection, authors of a meta-analysis found that 39% underwent surgical salvage of the infected breast implants of which 84.6% (95% CI 74.9% to 92.2%) successfully retained the salvaged implants without infection recurrence. Of the 35% who underwent explantation of the infected breast implant, only 39% chose to have re-insertion of a new implant on a later date and 5% of those patients had recurrence of infection requiring removal of the infected implant.

For recurrent periductal mastitis, authors of one case series of 47 women reported that extended excision with transferring a random ipsilateral breast dermo-glandular flap resulted in excellent graft survival and primary healing with an adequate to excellent patient-assessed cosmetic result in 89%. In another case series of 18 women with recurrent periductal mastitis, total excision of the affected duct and the fistulous tract resulted in good cosmetic results with 2 recurrences.

Homeopathic remedies that have been suggested for the treatment of mastitis include belladonna, Phytolacca, Chamomilla, and Bellis perennis. There is no scientific evidence regarding the safety and effectiveness of these homeopathic treatments for mastitis.
Probiotic lactobacilli were superior to antibiotics for the treatment of mastitis in one RCT.
Breastfeeding or milk expression should be continued to facilitate proper drainage of milk.
Increase fluid intake.
If an abscess incision interferes with latch-on, a breast pump should be used until the wound is sufficiently healed to allow breastfeeding.
Applying heat to the breast before feeding may help milk flow. After feeding, cold packs can be applied to reduce pain and edema.

Use of a management pathway in one institution improved compliance with antibiotic guidelines, increased use of ultrasound assessment, and reduced rates of incision and drainage (8%-0.7% post intervention). Rates of hospital admission were unchanged.

In a case series of 37 women with idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, 27 cases resolved with observation only with an average time to resolution of 7.4 months. 5 women underwent removal of masses and 5 were lost to follow-up. Three women had recurrent episodes.
Following incision and drainage of abscesses, patients may report poor cosmetic results.
Also following incision and drainage, patients may develop a milk fistula with constant leakage of milk from the area.
Up to 10% of women with mastitis will develop an abscess.
Almost 1/5 of women will have a recurrence of mastitis within 3 months.
Women with a history of mastitis have a 3-fold increased incidence of mastitis when breastfeeding subsequent children.

Overall recurrence of IGM is 17.18% based on a systematic review of 71 studies with 4735 patients. These authors found recurrence rates for specific treatments of 22.5% for surgery, 14.9% for combined treatment, 14.7% for immunosuppressive treatment, 9.4% for observation, and 6.7% for antibiotic treatment.
Women with mastitis should be examined after treatment to ensure resolution of the infection. If needle aspiration is done, it should continue until resolution of the abscess.
Mastitis is uncommon in children.
It occurs most often in the first 3 weeks of life, when the neonate has breast enlargement from maternal hormones.
S. aureus is the most common pathogen.
In case series, the infection responds well to antibiotics.
